mcqs.q: Heat-activated denture base resins are polymerized by which technique?
opts: Compression molding
Injection molding
Light activation
Pour-and-cure
mcqs.explain: Heat-activated denture base resins are polymerized by the compression molding technique.

mcqs.q: A flask is defined as:
opts: A metal case or tube used in investing procedures
The act of investing in a metal case
The procedure of bringing two halves of a case together
A device for maintaining pressure during polymerization
mcqs.explain: A flask is a metal case or tube used in investing procedures.

mcqs.q: Flasking is defined as:
opts: The act of investing in a flask
A metal case used in investing procedures
The removal of wax from a mould by heat
The placement of resin within the mould cavity
mcqs.explain: Flasking is the act of investing in a flask.

mcqs.q: Flask closure is defined as:
opts: The procedure of bringing two halves, or parts, of a flask together
The act of investing in a flask
The final tightening of the flask carrier
The sealing of the flask before boiling
mcqs.explain: Flask closure is the procedure of bringing two halves, or parts, of a flask together.

mcqs.q: The denture flask used is described as:
opts: A split mould, ejector type, three piece
A solid mould, two piece
A split mould, injection type, four piece
A solid mould, ejector type, three piece
mcqs.explain: It is a split mold — a denture flask of the ejector type, three piece.

mcqs.q: In the three-piece denture flask, the DRAG is the:
opts: Bottom
Middle
Thin top
Clamp
mcqs.explain: 1. The drag (bottom), 2. the cope (middle), 3. the cap (thin top).

mcqs.q: In the three-piece denture flask, the COPE is the:
opts: Middle
Bottom
Thin top
Ejector plate
mcqs.explain: The cope is the middle piece.

mcqs.q: The thin top piece of the denture flask is the:
opts: Cap
Cope
Drag
Carrier
mcqs.explain: The cap is the thin top piece.

mcqs.q: Why must the trial dentures be removed from the articulator without damaging the master cast or the mounting?
opts: So the denture and casts can be precisely reattached to the mountings after processing
So the articulator can be used for another case
So the wax can be reclaimed
So the vertical dimension can be increased
mcqs.explain: Following processing into heat cured acrylic resin, the denture and casts can be precisely reattached to the mountings — which is the whole basis of the later laboratory remount.

mcqs.q: In flasking, the trial dentures are first invested in:
opts: The lower half of the flask with dental plaster or stone
The upper half of the flask with dental plaster or stone
The cap, with separating medium only
Silicone putty in the drag
mcqs.explain: Invest the trial dentures in the lower half of the flask with dental plaster/stone.

mcqs.q: After the first investment, the dental stone must be:
opts: Smoothened
Roughened to provide retention
Left untouched until set
Coated with wax
mcqs.explain: Smoothen the dental stone — any undercut or rough ledge would prevent the flask opening cleanly.

mcqs.q: What is applied to the dental stone before the next pour?
opts: Separating media
Monomer
Petroleum jelly mixed with pumice
Tinfoil substitute mixed with plaster
mcqs.explain: Apply separating media to the dental stone, so the two halves part at wax elimination instead of bonding.

mcqs.q: The second pour of dental stone is carried:
opts: Till the incisal and occlusal surfaces, so the teeth are exposed
Over the teeth, burying them completely
To halfway up the denture flange only
To the level of the ridge crest
mcqs.explain: Pour dental stone till the incisal and occlusal surfaces, then expose the teeth.

mcqs.q: The lid of the flask is pressed into place:
opts: While the investing stone is still soft
After the investing stone has fully set
Only after the first boiling
After the separating medium has dried completely
mcqs.explain: The lid of the flask is pressed into place while the investing stone is still soft.

mcqs.q: Reading from the bottom up, the layers of a completed flasking are:
opts: Lower half stone, stone cast, upper half stone, stone cap
Stone cast, lower half stone, stone cap, upper half stone
Stone cap, upper half stone, stone cast, lower half stone
Lower half stone, upper half stone, stone cast, stone cap
mcqs.explain: From the bottom: lower half stone, stone cast, upper half stone, and the stone cap.

mcqs.q: How long must the stone harden before wax elimination begins?
opts: 30–45 minutes
4 minutes
8 hours
15 minutes
mcqs.explain: After the stone has hardened (30–45 min), the record base and wax must be removed from the mould.

mcqs.q: For how long is the denture flask put in boiling water to soften the wax?
opts: 4 minutes
15 minutes
30 minutes
1 hour
mcqs.explain: The denture flask is put in boiling water for 4 minutes.

mcqs.q: Wax elimination is defined as:
opts: The removal of wax from a mold, usually by heat
The removal of excess resin from the flask
The softening of wax prior to packing
The separation of the flask halves
mcqs.explain: Wax elimination is the removal of wax from a mold, usually by heat.

mcqs.q: After the softened wax is removed, the remaining wax is:
opts: Flushed from the mould with a stream of boiling water, then cleaned with a soft brush
Scraped out of the mould with a wax knife and the residue left in place
Dissolved out of the mould with a flood of liquid monomer
Burnt out of the mould in a furnace at polymerization temperature
mcqs.explain: Remaining wax is flushed from the mould with a stream of boiling water, and the mould is then cleaned with a soft brush.

mcqs.q: After wax elimination, where are the artificial teeth?
opts: Still locked in the stone of the upper half
Removed with the wax and reset later
Loose in the mould cavity
Embedded in the lower half with the cast
mcqs.explain: The teeth remain locked in stone, held in the upper half exactly where they were arranged.

mcqs.q: The separating medium applied after wax elimination should be put on:
opts: While the moulds are still warm
Only after the moulds have cooled completely
Before the flask is boiled
After the resin has been packed
mcqs.explain: Apply separating media while the moulds are still warm, so it flows and dries as an even film.

mcqs.q: What is the purpose of the separating medium applied after wax elimination?
opts: To stop the stone bonding to the acrylic resin
To stop the stone bonding to the stone
To lubricate the flask halves during closure
To reduce polymerization shrinkage
mcqs.explain: This separator keeps the stone from bonding to the ACRYLIC RESIN — a different job from the earlier separator, which kept stone from bonding to stone.

mcqs.q: The polymer-to-monomer ratio for heat-cure acrylic is approximately:
opts: 3 : 1 by volume
1 : 3 by volume
2 : 1 by volume
1 : 1 by volume
mcqs.explain: A polymer-to-monomer ratio of approximately 3 : 1 by volume.

mcqs.q: Why is the polymer-to-monomer ratio set where it is?
opts: It provides enough monomer to wet the polymer particles without excess that would increase shrinkage
It provides the fastest possible setting time for a heat-activated denture base resin
It gives the maximum working time for packing the mould before the dough stage
It minimizes the exothermic heat released by the resin during polymerization
mcqs.explain: The ratio provides sufficient monomer to thoroughly wet the polymer particles but does not contribute excess monomer that would produce increased polymerization shrinkage.

mcqs.q: If too much monomer is used in the mix, the consequence is:
opts: Increased polymerization shrinkage
Incomplete wetting of the polymer particles
A mix too dry to pack
Failure of the resin to polymerize at all
mcqs.explain: Excess monomer produces increased polymerization shrinkage; too little leaves the polymer particles inadequately wetted.

mcqs.q: Packing is defined as:
opts: The placement and adaptation of denture base resin within the mold cavity
The compression of the flask halves in a press
The removal of excess resin from the flask
The filling of the flask with investing stone
mcqs.explain: The placement and adaptation of denture base resin within the mold cavity are termed packing.

mcqs.q: What is placed between the flask halves during the trial closures?
opts: A thin polyethylene separator sheet
A sheet of tinfoil
A layer of baseplate wax
A wet paper towel
mcqs.explain: A thin polyethylene separator sheet is used, so the flask can be reopened without the resin sticking to the opposing half.

mcqs.q: Trial flask closure is defined as:
opts: Any preliminary closure made to eliminate excess material and ensure the mould is completely filled
The final closure of the flask immediately before it enters the polymerization bath
The closure of the flask made just before it is placed in boiling water for wax elimination
The act of bringing the cap and the cope together over the packed investing stone
mcqs.explain: That is the definition of a trial flask closure.

mcqs.q: The excess material extruded from between the flask halves is called the:
opts: Flash
Flange
Sprue
Festoon
mcqs.explain: Excess material is carefully removed from the flask — this excess is the flash.

mcqs.q: How many times is the trial closure repeated?
opts: 2–3 times, till excess flash is removed
Once only
At least 6 times
Until the flask will no longer open
mcqs.explain: Trial closure (2–3 times) is done till excess flash is removed.

mcqs.q: The flask carrier is used because it:
opts: Maintains pressure on the flasks during processing
Applies the initial pressure for the trial closure
Holds the flask during wax elimination
Ejects the denture after polymerization
mcqs.explain: The flask is transferred to a flask carrier, which maintains pressure on the flasks during processing — the press applies the pressure, the carrier holds it.

mcqs.q: The polymerization cycle is defined as:
opts: The heating process used to control polymerization
The time from mixing to the trial closure
The cooling schedule after polymerization
The ratio of polymer to monomer over time
mcqs.explain: The heating process used to control polymerization is termed the polymerization cycle or curing cycle.

mcqs.q: The FIRST polymerization technique described is:
opts: 74 °C for 8 hours or longer, with no terminal boiling treatment
74 °C for 8 hours then 100 °C for 1 hour
74 °C for 2 hours then 100 °C for 1 hour
100 °C for 8 hours
mcqs.explain: The first technique uses a constant-temperature water bath at 74 °C (165 °F) for 8 hours or longer, with no terminal boiling treatment.

mcqs.q: The SECOND polymerization technique described is:
opts: 74 °C for 8 hours, then 100 °C for 1 hour
74 °C for 2 hours, then 100 °C for 1 hour
74 °C for 8 hours with no terminal boiling
100 °C for 1 hour only
mcqs.explain: The second technique is 74 °C for 8 hours, then increasing to 100 °C for 1 hour.

mcqs.q: The THIRD polymerization technique described is:
opts: 74 °C for approximately 2 hours, then 100 °C for 1 hour
74 °C for 8 hours, then 100 °C for 1 hour
74 °C for 8 hours or longer with no terminal boiling
100 °C for 2 hours
mcqs.explain: The third technique processes at 74 °C for approximately 2 hours, then raises the bath to 100 °C for 1 hour.

mcqs.q: What temperature do all three polymerization techniques begin at?
mcqs.explain: All three begin at 74 °C (165 °F); they differ in how long they stay there and whether a terminal hour at 100 °C follows.

mcqs.q: Why must the flask be cooled slowly after polymerization?
opts: Rapid cooling can result in distortion of the denture base
Rapid cooling leaves the resin under-polymerized
Rapid cooling cracks the investing stone
Rapid cooling discolours the acrylic
mcqs.explain: Rapid cooling can result in distortion of the denture base.

mcqs.q: The recommended cooling schedule is:
opts: Bench cool 30 min, then cool tap water 15 min
Bench cool 15 min, then cool tap water 30 min
Cool tap water 30 min only
Bench cool overnight
mcqs.explain: Remove the flask from the water, bench cool for 30 min, then immerse in cool tap water for 15 min before deflasking.

mcqs.q: When deflasking complete dentures, it is best to use a:
opts: Flask ejector
Plaster knife and mallet
Vibrator
Hydraulic press
mcqs.explain: A flask ejector allows removal from the flask without damage to the denture or flask.

mcqs.q: A remount procedure is defined as:
opts: Acrylic shrinks on changing from moldable to solid and has a high thermal expansion coefficient
The artificial teeth loosen from their stone matrix during the wax elimination stage
The flask carrier distorts the denture base while maintaining pressure during processing
The separating medium alters the fit of the base against the master cast
mcqs.explain: That is the definition of a remount procedure.

mcqs.q: Why is a laboratory remount necessary at all?
opts: Before polishing the dentures, so the polished surface is not ground through afterwards
After polishing the dentures, once the surfaces have been brought to a high shine
After the patient has worn the dentures for a week and reported on the occlusion
Only if the patient reports discomfort at the insertion appointment
mcqs.explain: Acrylic resins shrink when they change from a moldable to a solid form, and have a high coefficient of thermal expansion; in cooling after polymerization they shrink, causing dimensional changes.

mcqs.q: Laboratory remounting and selective grinding should be carried out:
opts: Before polishing the dentures
After polishing the dentures
After the patient has worn the dentures for a week
Only if the patient reports discomfort
mcqs.explain: Laboratory remounting and selective grinding should be carried out BEFORE polishing the dentures.

mcqs.q: After the index grooves are cleaned, the dentures and casts are sealed to the mounting stone with:
opts: Sticky wax
Mounting plaster
Cyanoacrylate
Impression compound
mcqs.explain: After the index grooves are cleaned, the dentures and casts are sealed to the mounting stone with sticky wax.

mcqs.q: The objective of the laboratory remount is to restore the vertical dimension of occlusion to:
opts: The level achieved with the trial denture
1 mm above the trial denture level
The patient's rest vertical dimension
Whatever level gives bilateral balance
mcqs.explain: The objective is to restore the vertical dimension of occlusion to the level achieved with the trial denture.

mcqs.q: What incisal pin opening is acceptable at the laboratory remount?
opts: 2–3 mm
0 mm — the pin must already touch
Up to 5 mm
mcqs.explain: A 0.5–1 mm incisal pin opening is acceptable.

mcqs.q: How are the premature contacts identified at the remount?
opts: By tapping the two articulator members together with articulating paper between them
By measuring the incisal pin opening against the incisal table with a gauge
By visual inspection of the cusps under magnification and good lighting
By checking the horizontal and lateral condylar guidance settings on the articulator
mcqs.explain: Tap the two members of the articulator together with articulating paper between them.

mcqs.q: The BULL principle stands for:
opts: Buccal Upper / Lingual Lower
Buccal Upper / Lingual Upper
Balancing Upper / Lingual Lower
Buccal Under / Lingual Level
mcqs.explain: BULL = Buccal Upper / Lingual Lower — the cusps that are selectively ground.

mcqs.q: Under the BULL principle, which cusps of the LOWER teeth are ground?
opts: The lingual cusps
The buccal cusps
Both buccal and lingual
Neither — only the upper teeth are ground
mcqs.explain: LL — grind the LINGUAL cusps of the LOWER teeth; BU — grind the BUCCAL cusps of the UPPER teeth.

mcqs.q: Selective grinding is continued until:
opts: The incisal pin touches the incisal table
All the articulating paper marks disappear
The pin opening is reduced to 2 mm
The dentures separate on the balancing side
mcqs.explain: Do selective grinding till the incisal pin touches the incisal table.

mcqs.q: On completion of the laboratory remount, the articulator should:
opts: Slide easily from working to balancing to protrusive and back
Lock firmly in centric with no excursive movement
Open 0.5 mm at the incisal pin
Contact only on the working side
mcqs.explain: Upon completion, the articulator should slide easily from working to balancing to protrusive and back.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT listed among the instruments and materials for removing dentures from casts and polishing?
opts: Articulating paper
Plaster knife
Acrylic burs
Felt cones
mcqs.explain: The list is plaster knife, acrylic burs, pumice, rag polishing wheels, felt cones and brush wheels.

mcqs.q: When finishing the borders with an acrylic bur, the operator must be careful to:
opts: Preserve the border width and contour
Reduce the border width to improve comfort
Round the border to a knife edge
Remove the border seal entirely
mcqs.explain: Be careful to preserve the border width and contour — the border was developed by muscle trimming at the impression stage.

mcqs.q: Pumice is described as:
opts: A light-coloured abrasive, extremely porous igneous rock formed during explosive volcanic eruptions
A fine metallic oxide powder used with felt cones
A synthetic silica abrasive manufactured for dental use
A sedimentary rock ground to a fine powder
mcqs.explain: Pumice is a light-colored abrasive, extremely porous igneous rock that forms during explosive volcanic eruptions.

mcqs.q: Which surfaces are polished with the wet rag wheel and wet pumice?
opts: The palatal, lingual, labial and buccal areas, plus the periphery
The fitting surface and the periphery only
The occlusal surfaces of the teeth only
The palatal surface only
mcqs.explain: Use a wet rag wheel with lots of wet pumice to polish the palatal, lingual, labial and buccal areas; the periphery must also be carefully polished.

mcqs.q: Why must you not overpolish the denture?
opts: You would lose the contours that were developed during festooning
You would thin the base until it fractures
You would raise the vertical dimension of occlusion
You would remove the separating medium
mcqs.explain: Do not overpolish and thereby lose the contours that were developed during festooning.

mcqs.q: A correctly polished denture shows:
opts: Rounded and smooth borders and a highly polished palate of the proper thickness
Knife-edged borders and a matt palate
Rounded borders and a deliberately roughened palate for retention
Thin, sharp borders and a thick palate
mcqs.explain: Note that the borders are rounded and smooth, and the palate is highly polished and of the proper thickness.

mcqs.q: After finishing, the prostheses should be:
opts: Maintained in water till inserted in the mouth
Stored dry in a sealed container
Kept in disinfectant solution until insertion
Kept in the flask until the insertion appointment
mcqs.explain: After finishing of the dentures, the prostheses should be maintained in water till inserted in the mouth, since acrylic loses water and warps if allowed to dry.

mcqs.q: The clinical procedures of patient visit 5 are:
opts: Denture insertion and the clinical remount procedure
The try-in appointment and denture insertion
Jaw relation records and teeth selection
Clinical remount and selective grinding only
mcqs.explain: Visit 5 clinical: denture insertion and the clinical remount procedure; laboratory: the lab procedure for the clinical remount.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between the laboratory remount and the clinical remount?
opts: The laboratory remount corrects processing error; the clinical remount corrects tissue-seating error
They are the same procedure performed twice over, for safety and confirmation
The laboratory remount uses articulating paper whereas the clinical remount does not
The clinical remount is carried out before the laboratory remount in the sequence
mcqs.explain: They correct two different errors, which is why both are needed.

mcqs.q: A technician polishes the dentures first and then discovers premature contacts at the remount. What is the consequence?
opts: The polished surface must be ground through and then polished again
The dentures must be reflasked and reprocessed
Nothing — polishing does not affect the occlusion
The vertical dimension is permanently lost
mcqs.explain: Remount and grind first, polish second — polishing before grinding simply means grinding through the polished surface and polishing again.

mcqs.q: During flasking, if the stone around the denture is left with undercuts, what happens?
opts: The flask will not open cleanly at wax elimination
The resin will not polymerize fully
The teeth will be dislodged from the stone
The vertical dimension will be reduced
mcqs.explain: Anything that locks the two halves together prevents the flask from separating cleanly, which is why the stone must be smoothened with no undercuts.

saqs.q: By what technique are heat-activated denture base resins polymerized, and what is the overall sequence of the procedure?
saqs.a: By the COMPRESSION MOLDING TECHNIQUE. The sequence is: FLASK the waxed denture, ELIMINATE the wax to leave a mould, PACK the resin into that mould under PRESSURE, POLYMERIZE it with heat, then DEFLASK, REMOUNT and POLISH.

ans.text: By the compression molding technique.

steps: FLASK the waxed denture
ELIMINATE the wax, to leave a mould
PACK the resin into that mould under pressure
POLYMERIZE with heat
DEFLASK, REMOUNT and POLISH

saqs.q: Define flask, flasking and flask closure.
saqs.a: FLASK — a metal case or tube used in investing procedures. FLASKING — the act of investing in a flask. FLASK CLOSURE — the procedure of bringing two halves, or parts, of a flask together.

head: Term
Definition
rows: a metal case or tube used in investing procedures
the act of investing in a flask
the procedure of bringing two halves, or parts, of a flask together

saqs.q: Describe the denture flask and name its parts.
saqs.a: It is a SPLIT MOLD — an EJECTOR-TYPE, THREE PIECE denture flask: the DRAG (bottom), the COPE (middle) and the CAP (thin top). The ejector design allows deflasking without damage to the denture or flask.

ans.text: A split mold — an ejector-type, three piece denture flask.
The ejector design allows deflasking without damage to the denture or flask.

saqs.q: Why must neither the master cast nor the mounting be damaged when the trial dentures are removed from the articulator?
saqs.a: Because FOLLOWING PROCESSING INTO HEAT CURED ACRYLIC RESIN, THE DENTURE AND CASTS CAN BE PRECISELY REATTACHED TO THE MOUNTINGS. Preserving the mounting is what makes the later LABORATORY REMOUNT possible — the processed denture goes back on the articulator in exactly the position it left, so the dimensional change caused by processing can be measured and corrected.

ans.text: Because following processing into heat cured acrylic resin, the denture and casts can be precisely reattached to the mountings. Preserving the mounting is what makes the later laboratory remount possible — the processed denture goes back on the articulator in exactly the position it left, so the dimensional change caused by processing can be measured and corrected.

saqs.q: Set out the steps of flasking in order.
saqs.a: (1) INVEST the trial dentures in the LOWER HALF of the flask with dental plaster/stone. (2) SMOOTHEN the dental stone. (3) APPLY SEPARATING MEDIA to the dental stone. (4) POUR dental stone till the INCISAL AND OCCLUSAL SURFACES and EXPOSE THE TEETH. (5) Paint SEPARATING MEDIUM on the stone again. (6) Use dental stone to FILL THE REMAINDER of the flask, and press THE LID INTO PLACE WHILE THE INVESTING STONE IS STILL SOFT.

steps: Invest the trial dentures in the LOWER half of the flask with dental plaster / stone
Smoothen the dental stone
Apply separating media to the dental stone
Pour dental stone up to the incisal and occlusal surfaces, and expose the teeth
Paint separating medium on the dental stone again
Fill the remainder of the flask with dental stone, and press the lid into place while the investing stone is still soft

saqs.q: Name the four layers of a completed flasking, from the bottom up.
saqs.a: LOWER HALF STONE, STONE CAST, UPPER HALF STONE, STONE CAP. The same four layers are used for the mandibular complete denture as for the maxillary.

steps: Lower half stone
Stone cast
Upper half stone
Stone cap

ans.text: The same four layers are used for the mandibular complete denture as for the maxillary.

saqs.q: Define wax elimination and describe the procedure.
saqs.a: WAX ELIMINATION is the REMOVAL OF WAX FROM A MOLD, USUALLY BY HEAT. After the stone has hardened (30–45 min), the record base and wax must be removed, so THE DENTURE FLASK IS PUT IN BOILING WATER FOR 4 MINUTES to soften the wax. The flask is then OPENED and the softened wax removed; REMAINING WAX IS FLUSHED FROM THE MOULD WITH A STREAM OF BOILING WATER; and THE MOULD IS CLEANED WITH A SOFT BRUSH.

ans.text: The removal of wax from a mold, usually by heat.

steps: After the stone has hardened — 30–45 min — the record base and wax must be removed
Put the denture flask in boiling water for 4 minutes, to soften the wax
Open the flask and remove the softened wax
Flush remaining wax from the mould with a stream of boiling water
Clean the mould with a soft brush

saqs.q: After wax elimination, where are the teeth, and why does this matter?
saqs.a: The TEETH REMAIN LOCKED IN STONE in the upper half, exactly where they were arranged. That is the whole point of exposing them during flasking, and the reason the finished denture reproduces the trial set-up.

ans.text: The teeth remain locked in stone in the upper half, exactly where they were arranged. That is the whole point of exposing them during flasking — and the reason the finished denture reproduces the trial set-up.

saqs.q: Two different separating medium applications are made in this procedure. What does each one do?
saqs.a: The one applied DURING FLASKING keeps STONE from bonding to STONE, so the two halves of the flask will part at wax elimination. The one applied AFTER WAX ELIMINATION, WHILE THE MOULDS ARE STILL WARM, keeps the STONE from bonding to the ACRYLIC RESIN. Applying the second one warm lets it flow and dry as an even film.

head: When applied
What it prevents
rows: keeps stone from bonding to stone — so the two halves of the flask will part at wax elimination
After wax elimination, while the moulds are still warm
keeps stone from bonding to the acrylic resin

ans.text: Applying the second one warm lets it flow and dry as an even film.

saqs.q: State the mixing ratio for heat-cure acrylic and explain it.
saqs.a: A POLYMER-TO-MONOMER RATIO OF APPROXIMATELY 3 : 1 BY VOLUME. This ratio PROVIDES SUFFICIENT MONOMER TO THOROUGHLY WET THE POLYMER PARTICLES but DOES NOT CONTRIBUTE EXCESS MONOMER THAT WOULD PRODUCE INCREASED POLYMERIZATION SHRINKAGE — a compromise in both directions.

ans.text: A polymer-to-monomer ratio of approximately 3 : 1 by volume.
The ratio is therefore a compromise in both directions.

saqs.q: Define packing, and describe the steps of resin packing in the compression molding technique.
saqs.a: PACKING is THE PLACEMENT AND ADAPTATION OF DENTURE BASE RESIN WITHIN THE MOLD CAVITY. Properly mixed resin is placed into the mould cavity; a THIN POLYETHYLENE SEPARATOR SHEET is laid over it; the flask assembly is placed in a FLASK PRESS and PRESSURE IS APPLIED; the excess material (FLASH) is carefully removed; and TRIAL CLOSURE (2–3 TIMES) is done till excess flash is removed. The flask is then transferred to a FLASK CARRIER.

ans.text: The placement and adaptation of denture base resin within the mold cavity.

steps: Place properly mixed resin into the mould cavity
Lay a thin polyethylene separator sheet over it
Place the flask assembly in a flask press and apply pressure
Carefully remove the excess material (flash)
Trial closure 2–3 times, until the excess flash is removed
Transfer the flask to a flask carrier

saqs.q: Define trial flask closure, and explain why a polyethylene separator sheet is used.
saqs.a: TRIAL FLASK CLOSURE is ANY PRELIMINARY CLOSURE MADE FOR THE PURPOSE OF ELIMINATING EXCESS MATERIAL AND MAKING SURE THAT THE MOLD IS COMPLETELY FILLED. The thin polyethylene separator sheet lets the flask be opened again after each trial closure without the resin sticking to the opposing half, so the flash can be trimmed away and the closure repeated.

ans.text: Any preliminary closure made for the purpose of eliminating excess material and making sure that the mold is completely filled.

The thin polyethylene separator sheet lets the flask be opened again after each trial closure without the resin sticking to the opposing half — so the flash can be trimmed away and the closure repeated.

saqs.q: What is the flask carrier for?
saqs.a: THE FLASK IS TRANSFERRED TO A FLASK CARRIER, WHICH MAINTAINS PRESSURE ON THE FLASKS DURING PROCESSING. The press APPLIES the pressure; the carrier HOLDS it. Without it the halves would separate as the resin expands with heat, and the base would come out too thick.

ans.text: Without it the halves would separate as the resin expands with heat, and the base would come out too thick.

saqs.q: Define the polymerization cycle and give the three techniques.
saqs.a: THE HEATING PROCESS USED TO CONTROL POLYMERIZATION IS TERMED THE POLYMERIZATION CYCLE OR CURING CYCLE. (1) A CONSTANT-TEMPERATURE water bath at 74 °C (165 °F) for 8 HOURS OR LONGER, with NO TERMINAL BOILING TREATMENT. (2) 74 °C for 8 HOURS, then increasing to 100 °C for 1 HOUR. (3) 74 °C for approximately 2 HOURS, then raising the bath to 100 °C and processing for 1 HOUR. All three start at 74 °C; the first never goes higher, while the second and third both finish with 1 hour at 100 °C and differ only in the time spent at 74 °C first.

ans.text: The heating process used to control polymerization — also called the curing cycle.

head: Technique
Cycle
rows: a water bath at 74 °C (165 °F) for 8 hours or longer, with no terminal boiling treatment
74 °C for 8 hours, then increasing to 100 °C for 1 hour
74 °C for approximately 2 hours, then raising the bath to 100 °C and processing for 1 hour

ans.text: All three start at 74 °C. The first never goes higher, while the second and third both finish with 1 hour at 100 °C and differ only in the time spent at 74 °C first.

saqs.q: How is the flask cooled after polymerization, and why?
saqs.a: THE DENTURE FLASK SHOULD BE COOLED SLOWLY TO ROOM TEMPERATURE, because RAPID COOLING CAN RESULT IN DISTORTION OF THE DENTURE BASE. The flask is REMOVED FROM THE WATER AND BENCH COOLED FOR 30 MIN, then IMMERSED IN COOL TAP WATER FOR 15 MIN; the denture base can then be deflasked and prepared for delivery.

ans.text: The denture flask should be cooled slowly to room temperature, because rapid cooling can result in distortion of the denture base.

steps: Remove from the water and bench cool for 30 min
Immerse in cool tap water for 15 min
The denture base can then be deflasked and prepared for delivery

saqs.q: How should complete dentures be deflasked?
saqs.a: IT IS BEST TO USE A FLASK EJECTOR, WHICH ALLOWS REMOVAL FROM THE FLASK WITHOUT DAMAGE TO THE DENTURE OR FLASK. After recovery from the stone, the dentures are ready for remounting on the articulator.

ans.text: It is best to use a flask ejector, which allows removal from the flask without damage to the denture or flask. After recovery from the stone, the dentures are ready for remounting on the articulator.

saqs.q: Define a remount procedure and explain why one is needed after processing.
saqs.a: A REMOUNT PROCEDURE is ANY METHOD USED TO RELATE RESTORATIONS TO AN ARTICULATOR FOR ANALYSIS AND/OR TO ASSIST IN DEVELOPMENT OF A PLAN FOR OCCLUSAL RESHAPING. It is needed because ACRYLIC RESINS SHRINK WHEN THEY CHANGE FROM A MOLDABLE TO A SOLID FORM; THEY HAVE A HIGH COEFFICIENT OF THERMAL EXPANSION, AND IN COOLING AFTER POLYMERIZATION THEY SHRINK, CAUSING DIMENSIONAL CHANGES. These faults are corrected by careful SELECTIVE GRINDING, and both the remounting and the grinding are CARRIED OUT BEFORE POLISHING.

ans.text: Any method used to relate restorations to an articulator for analysis and/or to assist in development of a plan for occlusal reshaping.

ans.h: Why one is needed after processing
list: Acrylic resins shrink when they change from a moldable to a solid form
They have a high coefficient of thermal expansion, and in cooling after polymerization they shrink, causing dimensional changes

ans.text: These faults are corrected by careful selective grinding — and both the remounting and the grinding are carried out before polishing.

saqs.q: Describe the steps of laboratory remounting.
saqs.a: (1) The PROCESSED DENTURES ARE REMOVED FROM THE FLASKS. (2) THE INDICES ARE CLEANED. (3) After the index grooves are cleaned, THE DENTURES AND CASTS ARE SEALED TO THE MOUNTING STONE WITH STICKY WAX. The index grooves — cut into the mounting stone before the denture ever left the articulator — are what make the remount exact.

steps: The processed dentures are removed from the flasks
The indices are cleaned
The dentures and casts are sealed to the mounting stone with sticky wax

ans.text: The index grooves — cut into the mounting stone before the denture ever left the articulator — are what make the remount exact.

saqs.q: What is the objective of the laboratory remount, and how is the processing error measured?
saqs.a: THE OBJECTIVE IS TO RESTORE THE VERTICAL DIMENSION OF OCCLUSION TO THE LEVEL ACHIEVED WITH THE TRIAL DENTURE. The error is read directly as the gap between the INCISAL PIN and the INCISAL TABLE; a 0.5–1 mm INCISAL PIN OPENING IS ACCEPTABLE.

rows: to restore the vertical dimension of occlusion to the level achieved with the trial denture
read directly as the gap between the incisal pin and the incisal table

saqs.q: Explain the BULL principle and how selective grinding is carried out.
saqs.a: TAP THE TWO MEMBERS OF THE ARTICULATOR TOGETHER WITH ARTICULATING PAPER BETWEEN THEM; the marks are the premature contacts. These are then corrected with SELECTIVE GRINDING using the BULL PRINCIPLE — BUCCAL UPPER / LINGUAL LOWER: grind the BUCCAL cusps of the UPPER teeth and the LINGUAL cusps of the LOWER teeth. These are the NON-SUPPORTING cusps, so grinding them corrects the excursion without destroying the centric stops. Continue until THE INCISAL PIN TOUCHES THE INCISAL TABLE.

steps: Tap the two members of the articulator together with articulating paper between them — the marks are the premature contacts
Correct them with selective grinding, using the BULL principle
Continue until the incisal pin touches the incisal table

ans.text: These are the non-supporting cusps — so grinding them corrects the excursion without destroying the centric stops.

saqs.q: How do you know the laboratory remount is complete?
saqs.a: UPON COMPLETION, THE ARTICULATOR SHOULD SLIDE EASILY FROM WORKING TO BALANCING TO PROTRUSIVE AND BACK — balanced articulation restored after processing, with contact maintained in centric, working, balancing and protrusive, exactly as at the try-in.

ans.text: Upon completion, the articulator should slide easily from working to balancing to protrusive and back — balanced articulation restored after processing, with contact maintained in centric, working, balancing and protrusive, exactly as at the try-in.

saqs.q: List the instruments and materials used for removing dentures from casts and polishing.
saqs.a: PLASTER KNIFE, ACRYLIC BURS, PUMICE, RAG POLISHING WHEELS, FELT CONES and BRUSH WHEELS.

saqs.q: Describe the finishing procedure.
saqs.a: FINISH BORDERS WITH AN ACRYLIC BUR. REMOVE EXCESS RESIN BEYOND THE LAND. BE CAREFUL TO PRESERVE THE BORDER WIDTH AND CONTOUR. REMOVE ALL PLASTER OR STONE. SMOOTH THE DENTURE BASES TO THE PROPER CONTOUR WITH ACRYLIC BURS. The warning about the border matters because the border was developed by muscle trimming at the impression stage — trimming it away destroys the border seal and with it the retention.

steps: Finish borders with an acrylic bur
Remove excess resin beyond the land
Be careful to preserve the border width and contour
Remove all plaster or stone
Smooth the denture bases to the proper contour with acrylic burs

ans.text: The warning about the border matters because the border was developed by muscle trimming at the impression stage — trimming it away destroys the border seal, and with it the retention.

saqs.q: Define pumice.
saqs.a: A LIGHT-COLORED ABRASIVE, EXTREMELY POROUS IGNEOUS ROCK THAT FORMS DURING EXPLOSIVE VOLCANIC ERUPTIONS.

ans.text: A light-colored abrasive, extremely porous igneous rock that forms during explosive volcanic eruptions.

saqs.q: Describe the polishing procedure and its one prohibition.
saqs.a: USE A WET RAG WHEEL WITH LOTS OF WET PUMICE to polish the PALATAL, LINGUAL, LABIAL and BUCCAL areas. THE PERIPHERY OF THE DENTURE MUST ALSO BE CAREFULLY POLISHED. DO NOT OVERPOLISH AND THEREBY LOSE THE CONTOURS THAT WERE DEVELOPED DURING FESTOONING. A correctly polished denture has BORDERS THAT ARE ROUNDED AND SMOOTH and a PALATE THAT IS HIGHLY POLISHED AND OF THE PROPER THICKNESS.

list: Use a wet rag wheel with lots of wet pumice to polish the palatal, lingual, labial and buccal areas
The periphery of the denture must also be carefully polished

ans.text: The prohibition — do NOT overpolish and thereby lose the contours that were developed during festooning.

saqs.q: How are the finished dentures stored, and why?
saqs.a: AFTER FINISHING, THE PROSTHESES SHOULD BE MAINTAINED IN WATER TILL INSERTED IN THE MOUTH. Acrylic resin loses water and warps if allowed to dry out, and storing it wet holds the dimensions that the remount and selective grinding have just established.

ans.text: After finishing, the prostheses should be maintained in water until inserted in the mouth. Acrylic resin loses water and warps if allowed to dry out — and storing it wet holds the dimensions that the remount and selective grinding have just established.

saqs.q: Set out the procedures of patient visit 5, and distinguish the two kinds of remount.
saqs.a: VISIT 5 — CLINICAL: DENTURE INSERTION and the CLINICAL REMOUNT PROCEDURE. LABORATORY: the LAB PROCEDURE FOR THE CLINICAL REMOUNT. The LABORATORY remount corrects the error introduced by PROCESSING; the CLINICAL remount corrects the error that remains once the dentures are seated on the patient's own tissues. They are different errors, so both remounts are required.
